The same state as the Later Jin dossier (renamed Great Qing in 1636); this dossier begins where Cliopatria's Qing row does, with the 1644 realm of Manchuria, Inner Mongolia and Liaoxi as the core.

1644: Beijing and North China pass to the Qing. 'On April 24, 1644, Beijing fell to a rebel army led by Li Zicheng'; Wu Sangui surrendered on 27 May; 'On June 6, the Manchus and Wu entered the capital'; the Qing dynasty page: the dynasty 'seized control of the Ming capital Beijing and North China in 1644'. The pages name Beijing and 'North China', not a province list: this line takes Beijing from Li Zicheng (mirror of li-zicheng ledger/8); Hebei and Shandong follow on the next line and Shanxi, Henan and Shaanxi in 1645 (fx-09).

region.text: Hebei (Zhili) and Shandong, where the Qing repressed anti-Qing revolts

ledger.note: 1644: the Qing hold Hebei and Shandong. 'After repressing anti-Qing revolts in Hebei and Shandong in the summer and fall of 1644' (Dorgon page); the page gives no month and does not say who held the two provinces before, so the Ming (whose dossier still holds them after Li Zicheng's capture of Beijing) is the counterpart. Month 6 only orders the line after the Qing found of 6 June; the page says summer and fall. No mirror line in the Ming ledger: the Ming's own dissolve is dated April 1644 and its successor land goes through identity.successors (fx-09).
1645: the Qing take Nanjing, the Hongguang court's capital. The Southern Ming page: 'captured by the Qing on June 6' and also 'surrendered without a fight on June 8, 1645'.

1645: Hangzhou falls. The Longwu Emperor was enthroned on 18 August 1645 after Hangzhou fell (July 1645); the page does not name the captor in that sentence (the Qing is the researcher's reading). Zhu Yihai named himself regent in Zhejiang in October 1645.

region.text: Gansu as Cliopatria's Qing 1645 shape draws it (Lanzhou, Wuwei, Ganzhou), the part keyframes qing-dynasty_1646 and _1647 hold

ledger.counterpart: Ming remnants and local powers in Gansu (no dossier)
ledger.note: By 1646: Gansu is under Qing rule. Dorgon page: 'forces assembled by a Muslim leader known in Chinese sources as Milayin (米喇印) revolted against Qing rule in Ganzhou' in 1646, and Ding Guodong joined him. The page gives no date for the Qing takeover of Gansu (Xi'an was 'newly captured' by early April 1645), so the line carries the year 1646 only (the page's revolt is 'in late 1646' on a second passage, so Qing rule is older than that). Cliopatria's Qing 1645 shape holds Gansu a year earlier (fx-09). Review fx-09: narrowed to the 919 Gansu cells of Cliopatria's Qing 1645 shape (Ganzhou inside), which keyframes 1646 and 1647 hold; the whole province (1,705 cells) made the 1646 keyframe take 786 cells straight back out (keyframe_snaps 1646: 784 removed).

region.text: Zhejiang west of the Qiantang River, taken from the Lu regime

ledger.note: February 1646: the Qing take Zhejiang west of the Qiantang. In February 1646 Qing armies seized land west of the Qiantang River from the Lu regime (Southern Ming page).

17 October 1646: Fuzhou falls and Fujian passes to the Qing. after 'the fall of Fuzhou on 17 October' Zheng Zhilong defected; the Longwu Emperor was 'summarily executed in Tingzhou'; Koxinga went on resisting from the coast.

region.text: Guangzhou and the Pearl River delta

ledger.note: 20 January 1647: Guangzhou is taken. On 20 January 1647 a Qing force led by Li Chengdong captured Guangzhou, and the Yongli emperor fled to Nanning (Southern Ming page).

ledger.counterpart: Zhang Xianzhong's Xi regime and Ming loyalists in Sichuan
ledger.note: 1648: Sichuan is Qing land in Cliopatria's 1648 shape (71 percent of the province). None of the pages opened dates the Qing conquest of Sichuan: the Qing dynasty page does not mention it and the Southern Ming page gives only Huguang, Jiangxi and Guangdong for 1649-50. The year is the shape's (page silent).
1649-50: the Qing reconquer the middle south. In 1649–1650 Qing forces reconquered Huguang, Jiangxi and Guangdong, and Yongli fled to Nanning and then Guizhou (Southern Ming page).

24 November 1650: Guangzhou falls again. On 24 November 1650 Qing forces under Shang Kexi captured Guangzhou after a ten-month siege (Southern Ming page). The ten-month siege implies the city had been lost since the January 1647 capture; the page does not say when.

region.text: Guilin, retaken by the Southern Ming

ledger.note: August 1652: Li Dingguo retakes Guilin. In early August 1652 Li Dingguo 'retook Guilin' from the Qing; the page does not say when the Qing came back.

1659: Guizhou and Guangxi are Qing land again in Cliopatria's 1659 shape (100 percent of each). The Southern Ming page dates only the fall of Yunnan; the researcher bridges the two provinces to the year the Yongli court is driven out (page silent).

January 1659: Kunming falls and the last Southern Ming emperor flees to Burma. In late January 1659 a Qing army led by Doni took 'the capital of Yunnan'; Yongli fled into Burma and in 1662 was 'captured and executed by' Wu Sangui.

December 1673: Wu Sangui revolts in the south-west. 'In December 1673, Wu Sangui ended his connection to the Qing dynasty' and raised the Ming banner. The page puts Yunnan under the feudatories' control and lists Guizhou among the four provinces 'recovered' in 1680; that these two went first is the researcher's reading. Cliopatria draws the rebels as its 'Southern Ming' row (1673-82).
1674: Wu Sangui's forces hold Hunan and Sichuan. 'Wu's forces captured Hunan and Sichuan provinces' (the page gives no year, only the revolt's first phase; 1674 is a bridge).

1674: Geng Jingzhong rises in Fujian. 'In 1674 both Geng Jingzhong in Fujian' joined the revolt; the same year Zheng Jing 'led an army from Taiwan and landed in Fujian and Guangdong to fight and join the rebel forces'.

1674: Sun Yanling rises in Guangxi (and Wang Fuchen in Shaanxi). 'At the same time, Sun Yanling and Wang Fuchen also rose in revolt in Guangxi and Shaanxi provinces.' Wang Fuchen's Shaanxi rising ended after a three-year stalemate and is not drawn.
1676: Shang Zhixin joins the revolt. 'In 1676, Shang Zhixin joined the rebellion, consolidating Guangdong under his rule'; 'after 1676, the tide turned in favor of the Qing forces'.

1678: Qing forces retake the Hunan strongholds. After taking Yuezhou they 'captured it, along with the rebel territories of Changde, Hengzhou and others'; the same year Wu 'finally proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Zhou Dynasty' at Hengzhou and died in August (lunar month). The page names cities; the province is the researcher's reading.

1680: four provinces recovered. 'In 1680, the provinces of Hunan, Guizhou, Guangxi, and Sichuan were recovered by the Qing'; Sichuan and southern Shaanxi were retaken by Han Chinese Green Standard Army forces under Wang Jinbao and Zhao Liangdong.

1680: Fujian and Guangdong are back. The page dates no recovery: Geng Jingzhong and Shang Zhixin later surrendered; in 1680 Shang was forced to commit suicide and Geng executed, and Zheng Jing's forces were defeated near Xiamen and 'forced to withdraw to Taiwan'. The year is a bridge.

December 1681: the Three Feudatories revolt ends at Kunming. 'Zhao Liandong's army was the first to break through into Kunming' in October; 'Wu Shifan committed suicide in December and the rebels surrendered the following day.'

region.text: Taiwan and the Penghu islands, the Kingdom of Tungning

ledger.note: October 1683: Taiwan surrenders to the Qing. Zheng Keshuang surrendered in October 1683 and Taiwan became part of the Qing Empire; 'In 1683, Qing forces received the surrender of Formosa (Taiwan) from Zheng Keshuang' (Qing dynasty page); Tungning was 'defeated in 1683 at the Battle of Penghu' by Shi Lang (Qing conquest of the Ming page).

region.text: the Amur basin north of the river to the Stanovoy Range

ledger.note: 1685: the Qing drive the Russians from the Amur. 'The Qing won their first victory at Albazin in 1685'; 'By 1685 most of the Russians had been driven out of the area'; Albazin was overrun again in 1686.

region.text: the Amur basin north of the river to the Stanovoy Range

ledger.note: 27 August 1689: the Treaty of Nerchinsk ends the fighting on the Amur. 'The agreement was signed in Nerchinsk on 27 August 1689.'

region.text: the area north of the Amur River as far as the Stanovoy Range, including Albazin

ledger.note: 27 August 1689: the Qing hold the Amur basin to the Stanovoy Range. The Russians gave up the area north of the Amur River as far as the Stanovoy Range, which included Albazin; Russia kept the area between the Argun River and Lake Baikal. The border west of the Argun stayed undefined until Kyakhta (1727). Cliopatria draws the gain from 1691.

region.text: Khalkha Mongolia, held by Galdan's Dzungars from 1688

ledger.note: September 1690: Qing and Dzungar armies fight at Ulan Butong. Galdan 'destroyed several Khalkha tribes at the battle of Olgoi Nor (Olgoi Lake) in 1688' and held Outer Mongolia from the Selenga to the Khalkhyn Gol; at Ulan Butong the Dzungars 'formed a camel wall, beat back a pair of artillery-supported Qing assaults' and the Qing commander claimed victory. The Khalkha survivors fled south into Qing territory. The zone is Dzungar-held and fought over until 1696.

1691: the Khalkha princes submit to the Qing at Dolon Nor. 'The Khalkha rulers declared themselves Qing vassals at Dolon Nor' (1691). The Khalkha khanates themselves had ended under the Dzungar attack in 1688.

1696: the Khalkha vassalage becomes incorporation. After the war a Qing garrison stood near present-day Ulaanbaatar and Outer Mongolia was 'effectively incorporated into the Qing Empire'; the page gives no year for that, so 1696 follows Cliopatria's shape.

May 1696: Galdan is crushed at Jao Modo (Zuunmod). The Qing 'captured, killed or scattered all but 40–50 of the Dzungar army'; Galdan died in 1697 (suicide after the last defeat, or disease or plague, the page gives both).

region.text: Outer Mongolia, from the Selenga River to the Khalkhyn Gol

ledger.note: 1696: Outer Mongolia passes from the Dzungars to the Qing. Outer Mongolia was 'effectively incorporated into the Qing Empire'; Galdan had controlled it from the Selenga River to the Khalkhyn Gol. Cliopatria's 1696 shape also adds Tuva and more of Inner Mongolia, Ningxia and Gansu, which the page does not mention.

1720: the Qing expel the Dzungars from Tibet and set up a protectorate. The Dzungars were 'expelled by the Qing in 1720' after the 1717 invasion; 'a Qing protectorate in Tibet' with a garrison at Lhasa followed (1720-21); the 7th Dalai Lama was installed in 1720 or 1721. Tibet stays a separate Cliopatria row until 1793 and is drawn as vassal tint.

region.text: Amdo, made the province of Qinghai

ledger.note: 1724: Amdo becomes the Qing province of Qinghai. The page: 'made the region of Amdo into the province of Qinghai in 1724'; a Dzungar uprising there in 1723 was put down by Nian Gengyao (Dzungar-Qing Wars page). The pages do not name the previous holders; the Khoshut Mongols are the researcher's reading.

1726-27: eastern Kham is annexed to Sichuan. 'Eastern Kham was annexed to Sichuan in 1726-1727 through a treaty'; a boundary 'agreed upon by Lhasa and Beijing in 1726' was marked with a stone monument. Cliopatria's Tibet row loses the same land in 1727.

region.text: the frontier between the Qing and the Dzungars in western Mongolia

ledger.note: 1731: Qing and Dzungars fight on the western Mongolian frontier. In 1731 a Qing force was 'ambushed and annihilated near the Khoton Lake'; 'A Khalkha ally of the Qing Empire would finally defeat the Dzungars a year later in 1732.' The page names no zone: the frontier band is the researcher's reading.

region.text: the frontier between the Qing and the Dzungars

ledger.note: 1739: the Qing-Dzungar border is fixed by treaty. The two sides 'decided the border between them in a 1739 treaty'; the page describes no line.
1755: the Qing army enters Ili. In 1755 the Qing army under Zhaohui 'forced Dawachi to surrender' at Ili; Qianlong 'appointed Amursana as the Khan of Khoid', who resented it and rebelled.

1757: the Zunghars are defeated. The Qing dynasty page has the Kumul Khanate incorporated 'after helping Qing defeat the Zunghars in 1757'; the Dzungar-Qing Wars page dates the last battles (Oroi-Jalatu, Khurungui) to 1758 and Amursana's flight to Russia, where he died.

1757: Dzungaria becomes Qing land. Dzungaria and the surrounding area were added to the Qing Empire after the 1755–1758 campaigns (Dzungar-Qing Wars page, with 'the genocide of much of the Dzungar population in the conquered areas', undated); Dzungaria was conquered in 1759 on the Qing dynasty page. The year follows Cliopatria's shape and the 1757 defeat.

1757: the Kumul Khanate (Hami) is incorporated as a vassal. The page: it was incorporated 'after helping Qing defeat the Zunghars in 1757' and remained a vassal until 1930. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'Kumul Khanate'; the kumul-khanate dossier now exists.

1759: the Tarim Basin completes the conquest of Xinjiang. The Qing 'complete[d] their conquest of Xinjiang' in the 1759 campaign (Qing dynasty page); Xinjiang had been under Qing rule for a century after its 1759 conquest (Yettishar page); the Khojas of Us-Turfan 'submitted to the Qing Empire' after the 1758 battles (Dzungar-Qing Wars page). In 1762 the Ili General was set up to govern Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin.

region.text: Shigatse and Tashilhunpo, sacked by the Gorkhas

ledger.note: 1791: the Gorkhas occupy Shigatse. 'Again in 1791, Shigatse was occupied by the Gorkas'; the page dates the war 1788-1792, with Gorkha invasions of Tibet from 1788.
1792: the Gorkhas are driven back. Qing and Tibetan forces 'pursued the Gorkhas to the Kathmandu Valley, and Nepal conceded defeat'; no land changed hands.

region.text: the Nguyen kingdom of Vietnam as a Qing tributary

ledger.note: 1803: Vietnam under the Nguyen is a Qing tributary. None of the pages opened gives the start of the relation; 1803 is the first year Cliopatria's Nguyen row touches the Qing row (seed neighbour record), a bridge.
1842: Hong Kong Island is ceded to Britain. The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) opened treaty ports and ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain; the Qing surrender in 1842 was 'a decisive, humiliating blow'.

region.text: the Taiping zone along the middle and lower Yangtze

ledger.note: 19 March 1853: the Taiping take Nanjing and make it their Heavenly Capital. On March 19, 1853, 'the Taipings captured the city of Nanjing'; Wuchang fell in December 1852 and Anqing in February 1853.
1856: the Panthay Rebellion takes western Yunnan. The Qing dynasty page lists the Panthay Rebellion (1856–1873) in Yunnan; the Taiping Rebellion page gives 1855-1873.

region.text: the Amur's left bank and the Ussuri country, ceded or held jointly by the Aigun treaty

ledger.note: 28 May 1858: the Treaty of Aigun: the Amur's left bank to Russia, the Ussuri country a joint zone. Muravyov's treaty with the local Qing governor ceded the territory north of the Amur and made the area east of the Ussuri and south of the Amur a Sino-Russian condominium; Beijing refused to ratify it, calling it invalid. The date is inferred from the page ('signed 16 days earlier' than Putyatin's 13 June deal), so confidence 2.

region.text: Jiujiang and the rest of Jiangxi

ledger.note: 1858: Jiujiang and the rest of Jiangxi are retaken. Qing forces captured Jiujiang in May 1858 and 'captured Jiujiang and then the rest of Jiangxi by September'.
March 1860: the Taiping take Hangzhou, then Changzhou and Suzhou. 'The Taiping rebels were successful in taking Hangzhou on March 19, 1860'; Changzhou fell on 26 May and Suzhou on 2 June 1860.

October 1860: the Convention of Peking. The Amur Annexation page dates the two Convention of Peking treaties to 24 and 25 October 1860 and says they met nearly all Allied demands; neither it nor the Qing dynasty page (which says the Convention of Beijing was signed by Prince Gong) mentions Kowloon, so the cession of the Kowloon peninsula to Britain is recorded at confidence 1 (page silent).

region.text: the Amur's left bank and the Ussuri country

ledger.note: 14 November 1860: the Russo-Chinese Convention of Peking settles the Ussuri country. It ratified the Treaty of Tientsin and ceded 'all land north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri' to Russia.

region.text: all land north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri, the Pacific coast and Sakhalin

ledger.note: 14 November 1860: Outer Manchuria goes to Russia. The Convention of Peking ceded 'all land north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri'; the page's introduction adds the Pacific coast to the Korean border and Sakhalin, about 350,000 square miles (910,000 km2) over 1858-1860.

region.text: Anqing, the Taiping hold on the Yangtze

ledger.note: 1861: Zeng Guofan takes Anqing. In 1861 'Zeng Guofan's Xiang Army captured Anqing', aided by a Royal Navy blockade.

December 1861: the Taiping take Ningbo and hold Zhejiang. Ningbo was captured on December 9, 1861 (the same passage lists Hangzhou on December 31, 1861); Cliopatria's 1861 shape has Zhejiang almost wholly out of Qing hands.
10 May 1862: Ningbo is reclaimed. The Ever Victorious Army repelled another attack on Shanghai, and Ningbo was reclaimed on May 10, 1862 (Taiping Rebellion page).

region.text: the Wei River valley around Xi'an, where the Hui besieged the city

ledger.note: June 1862: the Hui rise in Shaanxi. After Zhang Fu was killed on 9 June, Hui armed groups surrounded Xi'an by late June 1862; in fall 1863 Xi'an was relieved and the Hui driven out of Shaanxi into Gansu; the Shaanxi Hui fled to Gansu in 1869. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'Hui rebels of Shaanxi (Dungan Revolt)'; the dungan-revolt dossier now exists.

October 1863: the Hui take Ningxia. Hui forces captured Ningxia Prefecture; Ma Hualong held Jinjibao from 1862 and Ma Zhanao's, Ma Guiyuan's and Ma Wenlu's movements began in Gansu in 1862. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'Hui rebels of Gansu (Dungan Revolt)'; the dungan-revolt dossier now exists.

region.text: the Tarim oases: Kucha, Yarkand, then Kashgar

ledger.note: June 1864: the Tarim rises. Dungans in Kucha rose on 3-4 June 1864 and Dungans in Yarkand rose on 26 July; Kashgar falls to Yaqub Beg in 1865 and the Yettishar page lists the seven cities as Kashgar, Khotan, Yarkand, Yengisar, Aksu, Kucha and Korla.

region.text: the last Taiping land around Nanjing

ledger.note: July 1864: Nanjing falls to the imperial armies and the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom ends. 'Nanjing fell in July 1864 to the imperial armies'; Hong Xiuquan died in June 1864.

region.text: the rest of Dzungaria, west and east of Urumqi, without the Urumqi district (dungan-revolt) and the Ili valley (ili-sultanate, from November 1864)

ledger.counterpart: Dungan and Taranchi rebels of Dzungaria (no dossier)
ledger.note: Summer to autumn 1864: the rebels take Dzungaria. Dungan Revolt page: 'Taking the cities of Manas (also known then as Suilai) on July 17', the Manchu fort at Manas fell on 16 September and Wusu on 29 September, the Dungans of the Ili Basin rose by early fall (all 1864), and Urumqi fell on 3 October (the line above). Tacheng's armory was seized around Chinese New Year 1865; the page does not mention Hami, Kumul or Turfan. The rest of Dzungaria is taken out with them, as Cliopatria's 1864 shape draws it (96 percent of Xinjiang out); no dossier holds this land, so the counterpart is a name (fx-09).

region.text: the Manchu fortress of Urumqi and its district

ledger.note: 3 October 1864: the Urumqi fortress falls. The Manchu fortress of Ürümqi fell to the joint Ürümqi and Kuchean rebels after the Urumqi garrison's Dungans rebelled on 26 June (page: 'The Dungan soldiers of the Ürümqi garrison rebelled on June 26, 1864'). Region narrowed in fx-09 to the Urumqi district, as the dungan-revolt ledger/9 gains it: a loss is skipped when the counterpart's dossier carries a gain in the same year, so the old whole-of-Dzungaria region left Dzungaria Qing in the compile; the rest of Dzungaria is the next line. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'Dungan rebels of Urumqi (Dungan Revolt)'; the dungan-revolt dossier now exists.
1865: Yaqub Beg takes Kashgar. Yaqub Beg, with Buzurg Khoja, took the Manchu fortress and town of Kashgar; Kokandian soldiers reached his borders in September 1865.

3 March 1866: Qing rule in the Ili Valley ends. Most of Huiyuan fell on 8 January 1866; Mingsioi blew up his mansion as the rebels broke into the citadel on 3 March, ending Qing rule in the Ili Valley for the time being. The Ili Sultanate is the researcher's name for the regime.

1869: the Hui are cleared from Shaanxi. Zuo defeated the Nian rebels by 1868 and the Shaanxi Hui fled to Gansu in 1869 (Dungan Revolt page). Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'Hui rebels of Shaanxi (Dungan Revolt)'; the dungan-revolt dossier now exists.

1871: Russia occupies the Ili Valley. None of the pages opened gives the year: the Yettishar page says only that the Ili region 'was returned by Russia to China under the 1881 Treaty of Saint Petersburg' and the Dungan Revolt page does not mention the occupation. 1871 is the researcher's recollection, recorded at confidence 1 (page silent).

January 1871: Ma Hualong surrenders at Jinjibao. Ma Hualong surrendered after a sixteen-month siege and was sentenced to death by slicing. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'Hui rebels of Gansu (Dungan Revolt)'; the dungan-revolt dossier now exists.

Late 1872: Xining falls. Xining fell in late 1872 after a three-month siege. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'Hui rebels of Gansu (Dungan Revolt)'; the dungan-revolt dossier now exists.

1873: the Panthay Rebellion ends and Yunnan is whole. The Qing dynasty page gives the Panthay Rebellion (1856–1873) in Yunnan; Cliopatria's Panthay row ends in 1872 and its Qing shape regains Yunnan (98 percent) in 1873.

24 October 1873: Suzhou (Jiuquan) falls to Zuo Zongtang's siege guns, securing the Hexi Corridor. The page names the city; the corridor is the researcher's reading. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'Hui rebels of Gansu (Dungan Revolt)'; the dungan-revolt dossier now exists.

August 1876: the Qing retake Urumqi and Dzungaria. 'In August 1876, the Qing appeared at Urumchi'; 'The place soon surrendered and the garrison was massacred' (a footnote: 'on 18 August, Urumchi fell without resistance'); Manas, north of Urumqi, 'On 6 November it surrendered' (Qing reconquest of Xinjiang page). The page does not name the holder; the dungan-revolt dossier has the Dungan state losing Urumqi in August 1876. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): was 1877 at confidence 1 (the year of Cliopatria's shape) with counterpart 'Dungan rebels of Urumqi (Dungan Revolt)'.

region.text: the Tarim oases, Yettishar's seven cities

ledger.note: 18 December 1877: the Qing enter Kashgar and Yettishar ends. On 18 December 1877 the Qing army entered Kashgar and 'brought the state to an end'; Yaqub Beg, per Musa Sayrami, was 'poisoned on 30 May 1877 in Korla'.
1881: Russia returns the Ili region. It 'was returned by Russia to China under the 1881 Treaty of Saint Petersburg'; Cliopatria draws the return in 1885.

1885: the Treaty of Tientsin ends Chinese suzerainty over Vietnam. The Sino-French War ended with the Treaty of Tientsin (1885), which recognised the French protectorate in Vietnam; France began expanding in Indochina in 1858.

region.text: Joseon Korea, a Qing tributary until 1895

ledger.note: 17 April 1895: the Qing lose Korea. By the Treaty of Shimonoseki 'Qing lost suzerainty over Korea'; 'Before the war, Korea remained one of the Qing tributary states'. The Unequal treaty page: the 1882 China-Korea treaty stipulated that 'Korea was a dependency of China', and 'Qing China lost its influence over Korea following the First Sino-Japanese War in 1895'.

17 April 1895: Taiwan is ceded to Japan. The Treaty of Shimonoseki 'ceded Taiwan and the Penghu Islands to Japan'; the Liaodong Peninsula was ceded too but 'returned by the Triple Intervention' (not drawn: Cliopatria's shape keeps it).

1898: Germany leases Jiaozhou Bay. The page: Germany leased Jiaozhou Bay. A lease, not a cession: drawn as occupation. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'german-empire'; the kiautschou-bay-leased-territory dossier now exists and holds the leased land from 1898.

region.text: the Liaodong (Kwantung) peninsula, Port Arthur and Dalny

ledger.note: 1898: Russia leases Liaodong. The page: Russia leased Liaodong. A lease, not a cession: drawn as occupation. The Russian invasion page: Russia held Liaotung from 1898. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'russian-empire'; the kwantung-leased-territory dossier now exists and holds the leased land from 1898. The Kwantung Leased Territory page: 'In March 1898 Russia formally leased the region for 25 years from China.'

region.text: the New Territories of Hong Kong

ledger.note: 1898: Britain leases the New Territories. The page: Britain leased the New Territories of Hong Kong. A lease, not a cession: drawn as occupation.

1898: France leases Guangzhouwan. The page: France leased Guangzhouwan. A lease, not a cession: drawn as occupation. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'french-indochina'; the guangzhouwan dossier now exists and holds the leased land from 1898.

29 June 1900: Russia invades Manchuria. 'On June 29 (1900), the first Russian force' crossed the border from Khabarovsk; Aigun fell on 22 July; the page puts the invasion at June-November 1900 and Manchuria 'partially' and later 'mostly' occupied, but 'His Majesty decided not to annex any part of China'. Occupation (hatched), not loss.

1905: the Russian occupation of Manchuria ends in Cliopatria's shape. The Russian invasion page says Russian occupation 'caus[ed] tensions that led to' the Russo-Japanese War (1904-05) and gives no end date or return; 1905 is the shape's year (page silent).

February 1910: Qing troops enter Lhasa. 'In February 1910, the Qing General Zhong Ying sent another army to Tibet'; 'The Qing forces occupied Lhasa in 1910' and the 13th Dalai Lama fled to India. Zhao Erfeng's campaigns in Kham and Amdo (1905 or 1908 on) are not drawn.

1911: Outer Mongolia leaves the Qing. The Qing dynasty page's infobox lists the Bogd Khanate among the successors but the text gives no date or events for Outer Mongolia; December 1911 is the researcher's recollection, recorded at confidence 1 (page silent). Cliopatria's 1912 Republic of China shape still contains Mongolia and has no Bogd Khanate row.

1912: the Qing garrison at Lhasa surrenders. 'the Qing amban submitted a formal letter of surrender to the Dalai Lama in the summer of 1912'; on 13 February 1913 the Dalai Lama declared independence and 'The amban and China's military were expelled'. The dynasty had fallen in February.
1912: Tibet's tie to the Qing ends with the dynasty. The amban's surrender in the summer of 1912 and the 1913 declaration of independence are on the page; the Cliopatria Tibet row resumes in 1912.

1912: the Kumul Khanate passes to the Republic. The Qing dynasty page says it remained a vassal until 1930. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'Kumul Khanate'; the kumul-khanate dossier now exists.

1912: the lease of Jiaozhou Bay outlives the dynasty and passes to the Republic (the end here is the Qing's, not the lease's). Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'german-empire'; the kiautschou-bay-leased-territory dossier now exists and holds the leased land from 1898.

1912: the Kwantung lease outlives the dynasty (the end here is the Qing's, not the lease's). The leaseholder changed in 1905: 'Under the Portsmouth Treaty (1905) resulting from the Russo-Japanese War, Japan replaced Russia as leaseholder' (Kwantung Leased Territory page); the kwantung-leased-territory dossier carries that change. Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'russian-empire', which kept the Russian lease to 1912 although Japan held it from 1905.
1912: the lease of the New Territories outlives the dynasty and passes to the Republic (the end here is the Qing's, not the lease's).

1912: the lease of Guangzhouwan outlives the dynasty and passes to the Republic (the end here is the Qing's, not the lease's). Reviewer fix (ea-08-b review, 2026-10-25): counterpart was 'french-indochina'; the guangzhouwan dossier now exists and holds the leased land from 1898.

region.text: the last Qing shape, passing to the Republic of China, with Outer Mongolia (Bogd Khanate) and Tibet seceding

ledger.note: 12 February 1912: the last emperor abdicates and the Qing ends. 'On 12 February 1912, Longyu issued the abdication of the child emperor Puyi'; the Republic of China had been created at Nanjing on 1 January 1912; the Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911 had set off the revolt of 14 of the 22 provinces. Successors in identity.successors.

wars.name: Qing conquest of the Ming
wars.outcome: Qing victory: Beijing and North China in 1644, Nanjing in June 1645, Fuzhou on 17 October 1646, Guangzhou in 1647 and 1650, Yunnan in January 1659; the Yongli Emperor was executed in 1662. Koxinga's Taiwan held out to 1683.
wars.note: The page has no dated map of 1645-1683 ('completing the conquest of China proper took another seventeen years', Qing dynasty page); the steps are from the Southern Ming page (also opened).

wars.name: Revolt of the Three Feudatories
wars.outcome: Qing victory after eight years: Hunan retaken 1678, four provinces in 1680, Kunming in October 1681, the rebels surrender in December 1681; 'By 1681, the Qing government had established control over a ravaged southern China' (Qing dynasty page).
wars.note: Cliopatria draws the rebels as its 'Southern Ming' row (1673-82). Wang Fuchen's Shaanxi rising and the Chahar revolt (undated) are not drawn.

wars.name: Battle of Penghu
wars.outcome: Qing victory: Tungning was 'defeated in 1683 at the Battle of Penghu' by Shi Lang; Zheng Keshuang surrendered in October 1683 and Taiwan became Qing land.

wars.name: Sino-Russian border conflicts

zones.text: the Amur basin north of the river to the Stanovoy Range

wars.outcome: Qing victory at Albazin (1685, 1686) and the Treaty of Nerchinsk of 27 August 1689: the Qing hold the Amur basin to the Stanovoy Range, Russia the Argun-Baikal country; the border west of the Argun was fixed at Kyakhta in 1727.
wars.note: The page gives the fighting as the Qing's first victory at Albazin in 1685 and the town overrun again in 1686.

wars.name: Dzungar–Qing Wars
wars.outcome: Qing victory: the Khalkha submit at Dolon Nor (1691), Galdan is crushed at Jao Modo (May 1696), the Dzungars are expelled from Tibet (1720), the border is fixed by a treaty (1739), Dzungaria is added after the 1755-1758 campaigns and the Dzungar population largely destroyed; the Tarim Basin follows in 1759.
wars.note: The page's infobox span is 1687-1758; the 1759 Tarim step is on the Qing dynasty page.

wars.name: Sino-Nepalese War

zones.text: Shigatse, occupied by the Gorkhas in 1791

wars.outcome: Qing and Tibetan victory: the Gorkhas, who sacked Tashilhunpo in 1791, were pursued to the Kathmandu Valley and 'Nepal conceded defeat'; no land changed hands.
wars.note: The page dates the war 1788-1792; the war's own article was not opened.

wars.name: First Opium War
wars.outcome: British victory: the Treaty of Nanjing (1842) opened treaty ports and ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain.

wars.name: Taiping Rebellion

zones.text: the Taiping zone at its peak, 1860-61

wars.outcome: Qing victory: Nanjing fell to the imperial armies in July 1864; Hong Xiuquan had died in June; the last Taiping army was destroyed in August 1871.
wars.note: The Qing dynasty page gives the rebellion as 1850-1864 in one place and 1849-1864 in another; the Taiping Rebellion page opens with the Jintian uprising of January 1851.

wars.name: Nian Rebellion
wars.outcome: Suppressed by 1868 (Zuo defeated the Nian rebels by 1868, Dungan Revolt page). An insurgency that held no drawn territory.
wars.note: Cliopatria's 1856 and 1865 shapes drop Shandong, Henan and Hebei for one year each; the pages show no such loss and the dossier treats both shapes as errors.

wars.name: Panthay Rebellion
wars.outcome: Qing victory in 1873; Yunnan whole again.

wars.name: Second Opium War
wars.outcome: Anglo-French victory: the Arrow incident of 1856, the Treaty of Tientsin signed in 1858 and ratified in 1859, Beijing captured in 1860 and the Convention of Beijing signed by Prince Gong; the Kowloon cession is not on the pages opened (ledger, confidence 1).

wars.name: Amur Annexation

zones.text: the Amur's left bank, the Ussuri country, the Pacific coast and Sakhalin

wars.outcome: Russian gain without a Russo-Chinese war: the Treaty of Aigun (28 May 1858) and the Convention of Peking (14 November 1860) gave Russia 'all land north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri', about 910,000 km2.
wars.note: Beijing refused to ratify the Aigun treaty; the Ussuri country was a condominium until 1860.

wars.name: Dungan Revolt (1862–1877)
belligerents: Hui rebels of Shaanxi and Gansu
wars.outcome: Qing victory under Zuo Zongtang: Shaanxi cleared by 1869, Jinjibao in January 1871, Xining in late 1872, Suzhou in October 1873, Kashgar on 18 December 1877; the Ili region returned by Russia in 1881.
wars.note: The Dungan Revolt page breaks off before 1876; the 1877 steps are from the Yettishar page (also opened).

wars.name: Sino-French War
wars.outcome: The war ended with the Treaty of Tientsin (1885), which recognised the French protectorate in Vietnam; the Qing lose their suzerainty over Vietnam, no Qing land changes hands.
wars.note: The page gives the war's end, not its start; fighting began earlier.

wars.name: First Sino-Japanese War

zones.text: Taiwan and the Penghu Islands, ceded
the Liaodong Peninsula, ceded and returned after the Triple Intervention

wars.outcome: Japanese victory: the Treaty of Shimonoseki (17 April 1895) ceded Taiwan and the Penghu Islands, ended the Qing suzerainty over Korea and ceded Liaodong, which was 'returned by the Triple Intervention'.
wars.note: The war began in July 1894 (declared 1 August).

wars.name: Boxer Rebellion
wars.outcome: The Eight-Nation Alliance invaded and the Boxer Protocol followed; Cixi fled to Xi'an in 1900. No Qing land changed hands in the treaty.

wars.name: Russian invasion of Manchuria
wars.outcome: Russian victory in the field, with Manchuria 'partially' and later 'mostly' occupied; Russia did not annex it ('His Majesty decided not to annex any part of China').
wars.note: The occupation lasted until the Russo-Japanese War (1904-05); the page gives no end date.

wars.name: Xinhai Revolution
wars.outcome: The Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911 set off the revolt of 14 of the 22 provinces by November; the Republic of China was created at Nanjing on 1 January 1912; Puyi abdicated on 12 February 1912.

certainty.note: The conquest of the south is provincial lines, the rebel zones of 1673-81 move yearly, and the Russian and Mongolian frontiers are undefined until Nerchinsk (1689).

Sharp lines: the Amur-Stanovoy line from the Treaty of Nerchinsk (27 August 1689), and the 1726 Lhasa-Beijing boundary in Kham (stone monument). The Mongolian frontier west of the Argun was undefined until Kyakhta (1727); the steppe, Xinjiang, Tibetan, Himalayan and Burmese frontiers stay soft.

Sharp: the Amur-Ussuri frontier (Convention of Peking, 14 November 1860), the coast and the 1898 leases. Soft: the Tibetan, Himalayan, Burmese and Mongolian frontiers, and Xinjiang's western frontier before the 1881 treaty.

Budget: 14 distinct pages opened (the budget for 61 shapes); three attempts failed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dzungar%E2%80%93Qing_War, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ili_crisis and .../Ili_Crisis: url_not_found). Nothing below rests on a search snippet; the few year-only entries recorded at confidence 1 say 'page silent'.

Start: the state is the Later Jin of 1616-1636 renamed Great Qing in 1636 (Qing dynasty page); Cliopatria keeps 'Later Jin Dynasty' to 1644 and starts 'Qing Dynasty' in 1645, and the Later Jin dossier (ea-08-a) ends in 1644 and asks this dossier to take over the colour and the Joseon tributary relation (done: vassal_start 1644, confidence 1). This dossier starts in June 1644, with a new keyframe for 1644. It ends 12 February 1912; Cliopatria's last Qing shape is 1911.

What was checked with the gazetteer (tools/gazetteer.py, the share of each province inside each shape): the 1645 shape is the Qing north of the Yangtze; the Southern Ming row of 1645-52 holds Jiangnan, Zhejiang, Fujian and Guangdong although the Southern Ming page has the Qing in Nanjing from June 1645 and in Fuzhou from October 1646 (keyframes 1645, 1646, 1647, 1648, 1649 corrected); the 1653 shape gives Guizhou, Guangxi and half of Yunnan to the Qing six years before the page has Kunming fall (keyframe 1653 corrected); the 1673-82 'Southern Ming' row is the Three Feudatories' revolt (3,615 of the 3,616 cells lost in 1673 and 7,724 of the 7,726 gained in 1683) and the revolt's real sequence (1673 Yunnan and Guizhou, 1674 four more, 1676 Guangdong, 1678-81 recovery) needed eight new keyframes; the 1794 shape adds exactly Cliopatria's Tibet 1793 shape, and the 1727 shape adds exactly the land the Tibet row loses (eastern Kham); the 1900-04 shapes remove all of Manchuria, which the Russian invasion page says was occupied, not annexed (keyframe 1900 corrected to the 1905 shape + occupation hatching); the 1856 and 1865 shapes drop Shandong, Henan and Hebei for one year each, which no page supports (corrected to the 1857 and 1866 shapes).

Infobox areas against Cliopatria: 1700 8.8 vs 8.89 (1.01); 1790 14.7 vs 11.3 (0.77); 1860 13.4 vs 10.5 (0.78); 1908 11.35 vs 11.1 (0.98). All inside a factor of two. The infobox seems to count claimed and tributary lands (Outer Manchuria before 1858-60, Kokand and Kazakh steppe).

Tibet: the page gives no status. The dossier draws it as a protectorate (vassal_start 1720, ended 1912) and keeps every 1794-1911 shape unchanged (status change only). The Tibet dossier (ea-06) must not also draw Tibet as solid Qing land.

Unverified for page budget (verdict ok, reason stated in each note): the 1687 loss of western Inner Mongolia and Ningxia, 1700 Qinghai at 54 percent, 1702, 1734, 1738, 1769 (the Sino-Burmese war was not opened), 1788-90 (+234 cells), 1814-1820 noise, 1822 (-611 cells on the western edge; likely Kokand), 1848 (-714 cells on the north-western steppe; likely the Russian advance), 1859 (Sichuan -12 percent until 1867), 1868.

Not covered by any page opened (gaps): the Joseon tributary settlement of 1637 (taken from the Later Jin dossier); the Ryukyu Kingdom's tribute and its 1879 annexation by Japan; Burma, Nepal (tribute missions), Sikkim, Bhutan, Kokand, the Kazakh hordes, Siam and Annam as tributaries; the 1765-69 Burma war; the Treaty of Kyakhta (1727) beyond what the Nerchinsk page says; Macau (1887); Port Arthur and Weihaiwei (1898 leases other than those in the Qing dynasty page); the Zheltuga Republic (1883-86, tiny); Hainan, Yunnan's western frontier and Taiwan's interior (the Qing never held all of it); the exact date of the Ili occupation (1871 is recorded at confidence 1); Urumqi's recovery date; the Russo-Japanese War and the Treaty of Portsmouth (Liaodong to Japan 1905); Zhao Erfeng's Kham campaigns (1905-1910); Outer Mongolia's declaration of independence (December 1911, confidence 1) and the Uryankhay Krai.

Counterparts without a dossier: Li Zicheng's Shun regime (1644); the Zhang Xianzhong / Xi regime and Ming loyalists of Sichuan; the Kumul Khanate (Hami); the Khojas of Altishahr; the Hui rebels of Shaanxi and Gansu and the Dungan rebels of Urumqi (Dungan Revolt; the ea-08-x batch writes rebel states); the Bogd Khanate. The Taiping, Panthay, Yettishar and Tungning dossiers exist already and are used as counterparts; 'southern-ming' (ea-07) is Cliopatria's name for the Three Feudatories in 1673-82, and ili-sultanate is the researcher's name for the Ili regime (the page does not name it).

Gazetteer names used or needed: 'Ili Valley' is not a region (Yining radius 150 km is used); the New Territories and Guangzhouwan are drawn with country Hong Kong and a Zhanjiang radius; 'Kowloon City' is an admin1 of Hong Kong S.A.R.; 'Suzhou' needs country China to disambiguate; Jiuquan, Jiaozhou and Port Arthur/Lushun are not place names (Qingdao and Dalian stand in).

Cliopatria rows: no row of this slug is to be split. The Opium War, treaty-port and leased-territory land (Hong Kong, Kowloon, Kiautschou, Kwantung, Guangzhouwan, Weihaiwei) is not in Cliopatria's Qing shapes except the three grid cells of Hong Kong; the concessions batch ea-08-x should add them as states with these counterpart events.
